items.title: Kid Cue is the iPhone Duo's secret weapon
items.content_html:
While some knock the iPhone Duo for perceived camera deficiencies, the Kid Cue feature might just be a big enough hit to make it worthwhile picking up for parents of kids young and old alike.

Like many, my choice of iPhone over the last decade or so has revolved around which cameras it has. As a parent of kids born in the mid-2010s, I wanted to be able to document everything in crystal-clear photos and videos.

The reality is that, despite what some might tell you, it's impossible to buy an iPhone that takes bad photos today. They're all great at it, and they have been for some time. The same goes for videos, too.

But there's no denying that models like the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max offer more flexibility. Even ignoring the new custom aperture situation, a real zoom lens is a big deal for some people.

The pro-tier paradox

With the iPhone Duo, Apple upset the natural order of things within its own lineup. No longer does paying the most money mean getting the best cameras.

If you want to pick up Apple's first foldable iPhone, you'll pay $800 more than an iPhone 18 Pro. Sure, it'll bend in the middle, but it'll take worse photos and videos in some circumstances.

This also means that if you do buy the model with the word "Pro" in its name, it'll be lacking. Pro cameras, maybe, but the iPhone Duo is the one that captures the imagination.

That's left a lot of potential buyers disappointed. But I'd wager that the iPhone Duo has a secret weapon, one that no other iPhone can boast.

Kid Cue uses the iPhone Duo's outer display to get the attention of kids when you want to take a photo or a video. And if you've ever tried to do either, you'll already know where I'm going with this.

The Kid Cue advantage

If you've ever been around kids, or dogs, for that matter, you'll know how difficult they can be. Things don't get any easier when you try to take a photo, no matter how many lenses or megapixels it has.

Kid Cue is Apple's answer to the age-old problem of getting a kid's attention long enough to snap a photo. When activated from the Camera app, Kid Cue puts a Snoopy-themed animation on the iPhone Duo's outer display to keep the child focused on the camera.

The iPhone Duo's Kid Cue mode is just a couple of taps away

While they're looking directly at the camera, you take the photo or capture your video. It's a simple feature, but one that should help avoid photos of kids looking in the other direction. The kind that litter any parent's Photos app.

Kid Cue is incredibly easy to use. And that's good, because you don't want to have to dive into settings when the chance for a great shot presents itself.

  1. Unfold your iPhone Duo with the inner display facing you.
  2. Open the Camera app.
  3. Tap the icon in the top-left that looks like the back of your iPhone Duo.
  4. Tap Kid Cue. The Snoopy-themed animation will play on the iPhone Duo's outer display to get your kid's attention.
  5. Take your photo or record your video as usual by pressing the shutter button or the Camera Control.

You won't get any of that with any other iPhone. And there's every chance it'll result in great photos that would otherwise never be taken.

Third-party alternatives

To be clear, Kid Cue is only available when using the official Apple Camera app preinstalled on the iPhone Duo. The feature isn't available for developers of other camera apps to use, but that doesn't mean that they can't get creative.

While apps can't hook into the Snoopy fun because there's no API available, they can mimic it. Developers are allowed to design their own attention-grabbing features using their own animations and graphics with the CameraCaptureAccessory and .sceneAccessory() APIs.

Whether they will or not remains to be seen. But the hope will be that Kid Cue is just the beginning, with developers using it as a jumping-off point for new ideas of their own.

A brave new world

The idea of the flagship iPhone no longer getting the best cameras is an alien one, that's for sure. But it's one that buyers will need to get used to, at least until bigger and better cameras can be squeezed into a foldable.

But the iPhone Duo's camera situation is more than serviceable, no matter what social media might tell you. And with that in mind, features like Kid Cue are very much welcome. The same goes for third-party iterations, too.

It could even be argued that despite its limitations, the iPhone Duo is the best iPhone for taking pictures of your family. It'll certainly help you capture shots of young kids that you might otherwise miss out on.

Just keep in mind that, for now, those shots might not be quite as sharp as they could be.

items.title: Donald Trump wants Tim Cook to be the next Nvidia CEO
items.content_html:
President Trump has weighed in on who he thinks Nvidia's next CEO should be, and he's picked another great big tech to do the job — Tim Cook.

The news broke early on Thursday morning about Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia. Whether he was told to quit or be fired, or if he made the decision himself may never be known.

Just the same, President Trump has chimed in on who he thinks should be Nvidia's next CEO. On a post on Truth, he has nominated Tim Cook for the job.

We got a screen cap of the post, just in case it changes or gets deleted.

Trump's post on Truth about wanting Cook to serve as Nvidia CEO.

It's not clear if Trump has talked to Cook about it, but that seems unlikely at this juncture. It's also unlikely that Trump has spoken to Nvidia's board about it yet, or if they will even consider the request.

Cook's got the chops to run the company, for sure. He probably also has significant non-compete clauses drafted following his exit from the role. Working for Nvidia would likely be a conflict.

And he's the chairman of the board at Apple. That seems to preclude the Nvidia job by itself.

If Trump does reach out to Cook, maybe Cook will suggest Johny Srouji for the spot. But maybe not, since he's done great work on Apple Silicon.

Not friends, but not enemies

During the first Trump administration, Cook was known for being close to the President, to a far greater degree than other business leaders.

During the term, Trump praised Cook for his communication skills, calling him a "great executive" due to repeatedly contacting Trump directly over important matters. While others used consultants, Trump was impressed by Cook's personal touch.

The term's famous US-China trade war was potentially damaging to Apple, but Cook led efforts to try and convince Trump from applying tariffs against its products. His influence certainly helped delay the application of tariffs, and did so altogether for iPhone, iPad, and Mac products when Trump signed a limited trade deal.

Outside of the trade war, Cook had visited the White House multiple times and discussed a wide range of topics with the world leader. Even a gaffe where Trump called him "Tim Apple" was taken in his stride.

And then, in Trump's second term as President, there's the "reciprocal" tariffs saga, that Cook spoke out against. That was followed shortly thereafter by the gold plaque gift.

Ultimately, those tariffs were ruled illegal. Apple has since received a series of refunds for those tariffs paid, which the company says will be reinvested in US manufacturing.

items.title: Nvidia only the latest to look towards Apple for salvation
items.content_html:
Whether you're in processors, entertainment, or cars, if your firm is tanking, all you'll hear is that Apple should step in, either with employees or a straight buyout offer. Even though it never does.

There was about a day between Nvidia's board meeting to oust CEO Jensen Huang and his resigning. You can guess what conversations were going on there, but you could also predict one thing about the world's reaction.

Before Huang even knew he was out, there were reports that he will be replaced by Apple's Johny Srouji. Those reports said Srouji was being considered and pointedly did not say whether Srouji had even been asked yet.

However, that wasn't the point. Maybe he'll become Nvidia CEO, maybe he won't, but right at this moment the point was to try moving the story along.

The moment Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's future was uncertain, Apple's Johny Srouji was said to be lined up as his replacement

If any company, anywhere, is losing millions of dollars by the hour, then like a Bat signal, the word will go out that Apple is needed.

Only Apple can save Nvidia. Or Tesla. Or Disney. The list goes on and will continue to go on.

That is partly because Apple is the most valuable company in the world and its pocket change could buy most other firms. This does make it a very easy answer when the question is who could afford to rescue this or that firm.

It's also partly because Apple doesn't have these calamitous financial missteps — or at least it hasn't since the 1990s.

Consequently, who you gonna call? Or if you have a problem and no one else can help, maybe you can hire Apple. Or someone from there, at least.

Apple-trained people

Trump thinks that Tim Cook should take over as Nvidia CEO. So along with Johny Srouji, that's two people who should step in to save the day there.

Yet OpenAI has hired at least 400 people out of Apple and that's not going so well at the moment.

Then the Humane AI pin was developed by two ex-Apple staffers and their history was enough to get them millions in investment capital. That also could've gone better.

OpenAI brought in ex-Apple design chief Jony Ive but so far has only released this photo of him and Sam Altman | Image Credit: OpenAI

So Apple people jumping to new ventures or being parachuted into existing ones is not a guarantee of success. But there's still how Apple could simply buy up just about any struggling company.

That's the easiest solution, or at least it appears to be the easiest answer for analysts who are asked about how to rescue firms.

It never happens

There is a problem with Apple being an easy answer for analysts and pundits and perhaps company directors, though, and it's that Apple won't do it. Apple never does.

Apple has acquired at least several hundred firms over the years, and right now it won't rule out making big AI acquisitions. But Apple does not acquire you as a favor.

It also doesn't have to wait until you're struggling. If Apple decides it needs your firm, it will just start what AppleInsider understands are ruthlessly tough negotiations.

Forget it. Apple won't buy Disney.

Consequently, while it's been true for a long time that Apple has the funds to buy Disney, it doesn't do it regardless of how low the sticker price gets. Disney doesn't fit, so Apple doesn't care.

For some reason, Disney is the firm that Apple is most often said to be buying. Or told that it should buy. Or rumored that it already has.

Back in 2009, Twitter was similarly in a position where it had clear strengths but was faltering, so naturally Apple was said to be buying it. Those particular reports, though, were Schrodinger-style because they all said both that it was happening, and that there was no evidence.

As it turned out, Twitter survived 2009 and the 2010s fine enough without Apple. Elon Musk stepped in, of course.

Now that you're thinking of Elon Musk, there is also Tesla. Analysts were absolutely certain that Apple tried to buy Tesla in 2013. They even specified that Apple had offered $240/share.

Elon Musk couldn't get Apple buy Tesla - Image Credit: Tesla

There is not one clue where that figure or those rumors came from, other than thin air. Especially since in 2019, Musk revealed that he had pitched selling Tesla to Apple.

Significantly, Tim Cook refused to even take the meeting.

It won't happen, but it won't end

Maybe Johny Srouji will leave Apple to go head up Nvidia. Maybe Tim Cook has already found that he misses being a CEO and the two will arm wrestle for the job.

But whatever happens with Nvidia, there will be another firm in trouble soon. And there will be another round of reports that Apple or Apple staffers are just about to step in.

So don't bet your own money on Apple buying Disney, or taking over Tesla, or its executives running Nvidia.

It might be interesting, though, to wager on whether cash-strapped OpenAI will be the next company to want bailing out by Apple. After all, Apple is trying to sue them into the ground over allegations of trade secret theft.

If it isn't OpenAI, it will be someone. And Apple will not buy them.

items.title: New AAPL $425 target bets big on unproven iPhone Duo supercycle
items.content_html:
China Renaissance has raised its Apple price target by over 50% to $425, betting that the iPhone Duo will spark a major upgrade cycle despite limited evidence that early demand will translate into sustained sales.

The Chinese financial services firm upgraded Apple from Hold to Buy on November 11, reversing a downgrade issued just 99 days earlier. China Renaissance previously cited rising component costs and slowing services growth as reasons for its more cautious outlook.

Analysts Jack Zhou and Lemuel Lin now believe Apple's first foldable iPhone could become a major source of growth. They expect the iPhone Duo to change how customers use their iPhones and potentially encourage earlier upgrades.

China Renaissance sees the iPhone Duo as an opportunity to drive growth over the coming decade, outweighing the financial pressures that prompted its earlier downgrade.

The analysts point to the iPhone Duo's larger folding display, multitasking capabilities, and Siri AI as potential reasons for existing iPhone owners to upgrade. Together, those features could make the phone more useful for tasks traditionally better suited to an iPad.

However, the iPhone Duo's multitasking capabilities remain more limited than those of an iPad, with no support for freely arranged app windows.

Another iPhone supercycle prediction faces an early test

China Renaissance's forecast is ambitious given how recently the iPhone Duo reached customers. Apple began selling the $1,999 foldable on October 23, leaving analysts with less than three weeks of sales history.

The company hasn't disclosed iPhone Duo unit sales, initial production volumes, or how many buyers are replacing existing iPhones.

Early interest has been strong, with delivery estimates extending into January 2027 after preorders opened. However, shipping delays can't establish the size of the market without knowing how many devices Apple can produce.

Apple CEO John Ternus acknowledged the supply constraints on November 2, saying production was increasing but the company couldn't predict when supply would catch up with demand.

Early buyers may be particularly enthusiastic about the new form factor. Broader adoption will depend on whether more customers consider a $1,999 foldable worth replacing their current phones.

Apple has also acknowledged screen failures affecting a small number of iPhone Duo units. The company is replacing affected devices, and the number is so far extremely small and not notably higher than infant failures of the iPhone 18 Pro.

Wall Street has made similar predictions before, and been wrong almost every time. Analysts expected the iPhone X to trigger a major upgrade supercycle in 2017, but the anticipated surge in replacement purchases never materialized.

The iPhone Duo could follow a different trajectory because its folding display introduces capabilities unavailable on conventional iPhones. However, higher revenue from an expensive new model wouldn't necessarily establish the widespread upgrade cycle China Renaissance expects.

Apple's financial pressures haven't disappeared

Apple's latest financial results demonstrate that its existing business remains strong, although the reporting period ended before the iPhone Duo went on sale. The company reported record September-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12% year over year, including record iPhone revenue for the quarter.

China Renaissance sees the iPhone Duo as an opportunity to drive growth over the coming decade.

Services revenue also reached a record $31.6 billion, although growth slowed to approximately 3% year over year.

According to Apple's financial filings, worldwide iPhone unit sales increased from 216.8 million in fiscal 2017 to 217.7 million in 2018, a rise of less than 1%. The July quarter's iPhone revenue told a different story, increasing 18% as higher average selling prices helped Apple earn more from roughly the same number of devices sold.

Rising costs are expected squeeze the profit Apple makes on each sale, with the company reporting a gross margin of 47.9% for the September quarter. Apple expects gross margin to decline to between 45% and 46% during the December quarter, with rising memory costs contributing to the pressure.

Ternus described memory pricing as unprecedented during the November 2 earnings call. Apple has partially offset higher memory expenses through existing inventory, lower costs for other components, and pricing increases, but further cost increases are expected.

China Renaissance, reported by Barrons, believes the iPhone Duo's long-term growth potential will outweigh those financial pressures. Its $425 target is among Wall Street's most bullish forecasts, exceeding Morgan Stanley's $350 target and Evercore ISI's $380 target.

items.title: Elizabeth Banks and Ted Danson team up for Apple TV's 'She's Fine'
items.content_html:
A brand new comedy series starring Elizabeth Banks is set to land on Apple TV on January 27, showing just how crazy life can get after divorce.

"She's Fine" follows Heidi (Banks), a recent divorcee, as she starts over for herself and her kids. Things go awry when she finds herself coordinating her father's retirement community sexcapades and forges an uneasy alliance with his girlfriend's single son.

The ensemble cast also features Rob Delaney, Ted Danson, Katey Sagal, Jared Goldstein, Spencer Moss, Titus Collier and Thaddaeus Collier.

"She's Fine" was created by Emmy Award nominee Liz Heldens and Matt Ward. It is produced for Apple TV by 20th Television.

The first two episodes will premiere on Wednesday, January 27. The remaining episodes will release every Wednesday until March 24, 2027.

The project marks Banks' second with Apple. In 2023, she starred in "The Beanie Bubble," a film about the driving forces behind one of the '90s' most iconic toys: Ty Warner's "Beanie Babies."
